what: Reduction wall time in seconds, process startup subtracted, measured by .github/workflows/stage2.yml in the SAIR-LEAN-KERNEL-CHALLENGE repository. Every variant ran in the same job on the same GitHub Actions runner.
route: The three designs below were timed with the obligation written `:= by rfl`, which routes the reduction to the kernel. An earlier version of this file reported figures taken with `:= rfl`, which has the elaborator's own definitional equality checker settle the goal instead, and described them as kernel time. They were not. The two routes differ by a factor of 478 at n = 18 on a list-based design and the elaborator route does not finish above that size; they agree on the packed design, which totals 0.07 s either way. The superseded figures were specification 48.40, lists 3.05, packed 0.07.
caveat: These are wall times on a virtualised runner, not instruction counts. The competition judge counts hardware instructions through perf_event_open, which a GitHub Actions runner does not expose. Only the ordering between designs carries over, not the numbers.

width_study.what: At the judged sizes the packed row finishes inside the timer's resolution, so the field width was tuned where the work is large enough to see.
width_study.route: These two rows were timed through the elaborator's checker, not the kernel. They are retained because the two routes agree on the packed design, so a comparison between two packed widths is unaffected; the wide-width variant no longer exists as a file and so was not re-timed.

judged.what: The competition's own metric, which was unavailable when the designs were chosen and has since scored two of them. These are the judge's figures, not a substitute for them.

per_operation.note: A one-word list operation costs more than a forty-three-word arithmetic operation, so the metric is not charging for operand width. Operation kind is what separates the designs.

substitute_accuracy.note: Both substitutes rank the designs correctly and neither sizes the gap; wall time is low by 1.6x and the step count by 3.9x.
